analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare to negotiate prices for the costliest brand-name drugs and caps seniors' out-of-pocket drug costs.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 230-192 on December 12, 2019, but the Senate never voted on it, and it expired when that Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let the Department of Health and Human Services negotiate maximum prices for insulin and up to 50 single-source brand-name drugs with no generic competition, capping those prices at 120% of what the same drugs cost in six other wealthy countries. It would also have forced drug makers to pay rebates when Medicare drug prices rise faster than inflation, capped Medicare beneficiaries' yearly out-of-pocket drug costs, and added dental, vision, and hearing coverage to Medicare. The House passed it, but the Senate never took it up.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries would pay less for the most expensive brand-name drugs, have their annual out-of-pocket drug spending capped, and gain dental, vision, and hearing coverage. Low-income beneficiaries would qualify for more help with premiums and cost-sharing, and the negotiated prices could flow through to people with private insurance unless their plan opts out.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors and people with drug coverage

how_it_helps.text: HHS must negotiate maximum fair prices for insulin products and, starting in 2023, at least 25 brand-name drugs without generic competition drawn from the 125 highest-spending drugs nationally and under Medicare, rising to at least 50 drugs in 2024. Current law prohibits HHS from negotiating drug prices.

The negotiated price may not exceed 120% of the average price in Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Japan, and the United Kingdom — or, where that data is unavailable, 85% of the U.S. average manufacturer price. Manufacturers that refuse to negotiate face an excise tax that escalates from 65% to 95% of sales, and those that break their agreements face civil penalties of up to ten times the overcharge.
Drug manufacturers must pay rebates to Medicare for drugs costing $100 or more whose prices rise faster than inflation, and must report price increases at least 30 days before they take effect.

Medicare beneficiaries' annual out-of-pocket drug spending threshold is reduced and cost-sharing above it eliminated, low-income beneficiaries get expanded premium and cost-sharing subsidies, and Medicare gains dental (including dentures), hearing (including hearing aids), and vision (including eyeglasses) coverage.

The negotiated maximum prices apply automatically to private group and individual health plans unless the insurer affirmatively opts out, and plans that opt out must disclose it publicly; federal employee health coverage cannot contract with carriers that opt out.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers bear the cost: lower prices on their biggest-selling drugs, rebates when prices outpace inflation, and steep excise taxes if they refuse to negotiate. Taxpayers fund the new Medicare dental, vision, and hearing benefit and expanded NIH, FDA, opioid, and community health center funding. Pharmacy benefit managers lose the spread-pricing practice banned in Medicaid.

drawbacks.text: Opponents argued that capping prices on top-selling drugs could reduce the development of new medicines. An amendment offered on the House floor would have delayed the bill's effective date until HHS certified that implementation was not projected to reduce new drug applications for unmet medical needs and lifesaving cures; it failed 196-226.

The negotiation program covers only drugs that are among the 125 highest-spending nationally or under Medicare, have no generic competition, and are single-source — so most prescription drugs would be unaffected.

The bill creates substantial new federal spending: a new Medicare dental, vision, and hearing benefit, guaranteed-issue rights for Medigap policies, expanded low-income subsidies, and added NIH, FDA, opioid, and community health center funding through the late 2020s.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Medicare beneficiaries and people with drug coverage, the benefits are large and direct: lower prices on the biggest-selling brand-name drugs, a hard cap on yearly out-of-pocket drug costs, and new dental, vision, and hearing coverage. The costs fall mainly on brand-name drug makers in the form of lower revenue, and on taxpayers for the new benefits. The strongest good-faith objection — that lower returns could mean fewer new cures — is contested and was not tested, since the bill never became law. The bill's main design limitation is that its price negotiation reaches only a narrow slice of drugs: those with the highest spending and no generic competition.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 230-192, but the Senate never voted on it — the bill sat on the Senate calendar from September 2020 until that Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: The House passed H.R. 3 on December 12, 2019, by a vote of 230-192: all 228 voting Democrats in favor, 2 of 193 Republicans in favor, and the chamber's Independent opposed.

Before final passage, a Republican motion to recommit — which would have delayed the bill until HHS certified it would not reduce new drug applications — failed 196-226, with 193 of 193 voting Republicans supporting it and 3 Democrats crossing over.

The Senate received the bill on December 16, 2019; it was read twice and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 521) on September 8, 2020, where it remained with no vote ever scheduled before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
The bill had 106 cosponsors, all Democrats.
Three House committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Labor — all reported the bill, with Energy and Commerce advancing it on a 30-22 vote and 24-17 vote during markup.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers came out ahead: Medicare remains barred from negotiating drug prices, and no inflation rebates, international price caps, or out-of-pocket cap took effect. Senate Republicans who opposed the bill also benefited, having stopped it without ever having to vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote was 228-0 among Democrats for passage and 2-191 among Republicans against, with the chamber's Independent also opposed; the bill then died in a Senate controlled by Republicans without a vote.

industries.note: The bill forces them to negotiate maximum prices on their biggest-selling drugs, capped at 120% of prices in six other countries, pay rebates when prices outpace inflation, and face an excise tax rising to 95% of sales if they refuse to negotiate. Their core revenue stream from unregulated U.S. pricing was directly at stake.

The bill requires pass-through pricing models and prohibits spread pricing — keeping the difference between what Medicaid pays and what the PBM pays the pharmacy — in Medicaid drug payment arrangements.

Private plans automatically get the negotiated maximum prices and must cap related cost-sharing, lowering plan drug costs — unless they affirmatively opt out and disclose it. Federal employee plans cannot contract with carriers that opt out.

A drug leaves the negotiation program once two competing generics or biosimilars reach the market, and the bill temporarily raises Medicare Part B payment for certain biosimilars, encouraging cheaper competition.
The bill funds NIH and FDA innovation projects through the late 2020s and creates an Opioid Epidemic Response Fund, channeling some of the federal savings into public health programs.
